Before Leamington RFC, there was Leamington Rovers.

Founded in 1876, 50 years before today's club, they wore black shirts with a skull and crossbones on the front, played on Leam Terrace East, and had 100 members by 1879.

They reached the final of the inaugural Midland Counties Cup in 1882, losing to Moseley. They folded in 1886 when members stopped paying their subscriptions.

A century and a half on, the skull and crossbones returns. The Vets and the Lions have been wearing it on our centenary away strip, in tribute to the Rovers.

It started with a meeting.

14 April 1926. Leamington Town Hall. Around 70 people attended, chaired by the Deputy Mayor, G.W. Hawkins.

The reason they were there: 15 to 20 Leamington men were travelling to Kenilworth to play rugby every week. Why not form their own club?

Fred Barr took the chair of the new committee. The history describes him as the father of the club.

The rest is 100 years of history. 💙❤️💛

facebook:1643647319253798_15625416558091.caption:
Leamington station, 1935.

The New Zealand All Blacks stepped off the train and into town. The club put them up at the Regent Hotel and threw them a dance at the Palais de Danse. Some evening that must have been.

Sixteen years later, the Springboks came through. 630 people packed into Chesford Grange for the dance in their honour. When they left, they gave us two carved Springboks as a thank you. They have been leaping across our clubhouse wall ever since.

Two years after that, the All Blacks were back. They trained at our ground before playing the Midland Counties at Welford Road.

And in 1957, the Wallabies followed.

Four of the most famous touring sides in world rugby, all of them here, in Leamington. And two of them still with us on the clubhouse wall. 💙❤️💛

In 1981, social secretary Trevor Roberts had an idea. Why not run the ball to Twickenham, like the Olympic torch relay, and raise some money on the way?

On 15 May 1982, a team of around 15 runners set off from Moorefields at 5am. Over twelve hours later, they ran onto the pitch at Twickenham. Robin Andrews had the honour of touching down.

They called it Running the Ball. It raised around £400, somewhere north of £1,500 in today’s money, with £225 going to Helen Ley House.

People enjoyed it so much they did it again. To Cardiff Arms Park in 1984. Across the sea to Lansdowne Road in 1985. Up to Edinburgh in 1986. Over the channel to Parc des Princes in 1987.

Every home union opened their stadium to a bunch of amateur runners. Every one except Scotland. Edinburgh Academicals stepped in and hosted them instead.

Over five years and five runs, several thousand pounds were raised for six different charities, including Helen Ley House, Leukaemia Research and Save the Children.

Italy hadn’t joined the championship yet. Maybe there’s some unfinished business.

Were you there? We’ve only got photos from the Cardiff leg. If you’ve got shots from Twickenham, Dublin, Edinburgh or Paris, we’d love to see them. 💙❤️💛

facebook:1643647319253798_16314618655837.caption:
🧠🏉 CONCUSSION AWARENESS DAY | 18 SEPTEMBER

Rugby is a physical game. We love the competition, the tackles, the teamwork and everything that comes with being part of a rugby club.

But there is one thing that will always come before the game: our players' health.

WHAT IS CONCUSSION?
Concussion is a brain injury. It can happen after a direct blow to the head, but it can also happen following a hit to the body that causes the head and brain to move rapidly.

And importantly, you don't have to lose consciousness to have a concussion.

Headache, dizziness, confusion, memory problems, poor balance, nausea, feeling foggy or simply not seeming like themselves can all be signs that something isn't right.

That's why everyone at Leamington RFC needs to know the 4 Rs: players, parents, coaches, first aiders, therapists and supporters.

🧠 1. RECOGNISE
Know the signs and symptoms. If something doesn't look right, take it seriously.

🛑 2. REMOVE
If concussion is suspected, remove the player from play immediately. There is no "playing on" and no same-day return to rugby in community rugby.

❤️ 3. RECOVER
Concussion needs time and appropriate management. Recovery should never be rushed, and players should follow the appropriate graduated return-to-play process.

🏉 4. RETURN
Returning to rugby is the final step, when the player is ready and has completed the appropriate return-to-play process safely.

OUR COMMITMENT TO PLAYER WELFARE
At our club, concussion awareness isn't just something we talk about on one day of the year.

We are proud to have:
✔️ 4 qualified physios and sports therapists for senior and colts rugby
✔️ A qualified first aider for every age group
✔️ Coaches, first aiders and therapists completing RFU HEADCASE training every year
✔️ A commitment to following RFU and World Rugby guidance

Because concussion can affect players of every age, from our youngest age groups through to senior rugby, everyone has a part to play in recognising when something isn't right.

If in doubt, sit them out.

The match, the training session and the result can wait. The player's brain can't. 💙❤️💛

instagram:18103222175059911.caption:
🧠🏉 CONCUSSION AWARENESS DAY | 18 SEPTEMBER

Rugby is a physical game. We love the competition, the tackles, the teamwork and everything that comes with being part of a rugby club.

But there is one thing that will always come before the game: our players' health.

WHAT IS CONCUSSION?
Concussion is a brain injury. It can happen after a direct blow to the head, but it can also happen following a hit to the body that causes the head and brain to move rapidly.

And importantly, you don't have to lose consciousness to have a concussion.

Headache, dizziness, confusion, memory problems, poor balance, nausea, feeling foggy or simply not seeming like themselves can all be signs that something isn't right.

That's why everyone at Leamington RFC needs to know the 4 Rs: players, parents, coaches, first aiders, therapists and supporters.

🧠 1. RECOGNISE
Know the signs and symptoms. If something doesn't look right, take it seriously.

🛑 2. REMOVE
If concussion is suspected, remove the player from play immediately. There is no "playing on" and no same-day return to rugby in community rugby.

❤️ 3. RECOVER
Concussion needs time and appropriate management. Recovery should never be rushed, and players should follow the appropriate graduated return-to-play process.

🏉 4. RETURN
Returning to rugby is the final step, when the player is ready and has completed the appropriate return-to-play process safely.

OUR COMMITMENT TO PLAYER WELFARE
At our club, concussion awareness isn't just something we talk about on one day of the year.

We are proud to have:
✔️ 4 qualified physios and sports therapists for senior and colts rugby
✔️ A qualified first aider for every age group
✔️ Coaches, first aiders and therapists completing RFU HEADCASE training every year
✔️ A commitment to following RFU and World Rugby guidance

Because concussion can affect players of every age, from our youngest age groups through to senior rugby, everyone has a part to play in recognising when something isn't right.

If in doubt, sit them out.

The match, the training session and the result can wait. The player's brain can't. 💙❤️💛

Ten Leamington RFC members nominated for the England Rugby Volunteer of the Year Awards. 🏉

We’re incredibly proud that nine members of Leamington RFC have been nominated for the England Rugby Volunteer of the Year Awards 25/26. Lucy Ramsbottom and Leanne Butters were at the Warwickshire RFU ceremony at Coventry RFC’s Nick Newbold Stadium yesterday representing the group.

Bill Dalton, Nora Mixova, Mark Pascoe, Harry Gooch, Julie Blackmore, Leanne Butters, Lucy Ramsbottom, Phil Evans, Hayley White, and John Raby - thank you.

Volunteers have kept this club alive and thriving for 100 years. None of what we do happens without people giving their time freely, week after week, because they love this club. It’s as true now as it was in 1926.

Congratulations to all nine. Well deserved, every one of you.

122-0.

March 1980. The Spartans against Stratford. 24 tries. The referee stopped the game well before the 80-minute mark once he knew the club record had been beaten.

It remains the highest score ever recorded by any Leamington RFC team, and still stands today.
Pictured: the Spartans squad from that season. Not necessarily the exact side out on the day, but the team that made history.

Were you there, or do you know someone who was? Tell us what you remember. 💙❤️💛

In winter 1949/50, Leamington RFC started using the gymnasium at Arnold Lodge School for training sessions.

Also using the gym was a young boxer from Leamington by the name of Randy Turpin.

The Leamington Licker.

A year or so later he would beat Sugar Ray Robinson at Earls Court to become world middleweight champion. Before that, he was practising his body shots on our players to toughen them up.

Photo: Turpin squaring up to scrum half Peter Jones, Arnold Lodge School gym. 💙❤️💛

instagram:18465033178102711.caption:
This Saturday at Moorefields.

From 12pm we’re hosting the Warwickshire Walking Rugby Festival on behalf of Warwickshire RFU. The festival has been going four years now, and we’ve won it twice. We’re back in it again this year, alongside clubs from across the county, and we’re proud to be hosting as part of our centenary celebrations.

Then at 3pm, we welcome San Isidro RFC, a touring side from Madrid, for a veterans’ fixture. Known back home as the Old Lizards, they’re here thanks to a club connection going back to 1994, when one of their players lined up alongside one of ours at Alcester. Thirty-odd years on, the friendship’s brought a Spanish touring team to Leamington.

All welcome for the rugby, all welcome for the social that follows. Come and be part of it.
💙❤️💛
